name: ผิวแพ้ง่ายเมื่อสัมผัส
pinyin: pí fū gǎn jué guò mǐn
preview_text: ผิวหนังที่เจ็บเพียงสัมผัสเบาที่สุดไม่ได้เป็นเพียงปัญหาบนพื้นผิวเท่านั้น แต่ใน TCM ยังเป็นสัญญาณจากรูปแบบที่ลึกซึ้งยิ่งขึ้นของลม ชื้น ความร้อน หรือภาวะขาดเลือด พลุเฉียบพลันส่วนใหญ่สงบปัญญา...
categories: ["สภาพผิว", "อาการชาและปัญหาทางประสาทสัมผัส"]
synonyms: ["Sensitivity of the skin to touch", "Skin that is easily irritated"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, skin that hurts or feels irritated in response to normally non-painful touch is often called allodynia. It can occur with nerve-related conditions (such as neuropathy, fibromyalgia, or post-herpetic neuralgia), with skin inflammation (eczema, contact dermatitis, sunburn), or when the central nervous system becomes sensitized after an injury or chronic pain state. The diagnosis is usually based on a physical exam and patient history, and testing may rule out underlying nerve damage or autoimmune disorders.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment depends on the suspected cause but commonly includes topical numbing agents, corticosteroid creams, antihistamines for allergic reactions, and oral nerve-pain medications such as gabapentin, pregabalin, or tricyclic antidepressants. For inflammatory skin conditions, moisturizers and avoidance of irritants are first-line, with immunosuppressant creams or systemic drugs reserved for severe cases.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the skin is closely linked to the Lung organ system and the body's Defensive Qi (Wei Qi), which circulates just beneath the surface to protect against external pathogens. When this protective barrier is weakened or breached, Wind, Heat, or Dampness can invade and become trapped in the skin, causing sudden hypersensitivity, redness, and itching. This is why many acute flares begin after exposure to wind, sudden temperature changes, or allergens - the surface has been caught off guard.
But not all skin hypersensitivity comes from the outside. Internal heat, if it builds up in the Blood, can agitate the skin from within, making it feel hot, red, and painfully tender even without an external trigger. This deeper heat often accompanies emotional stress, overwork, or a diet heavy in spicy and greasy foods. The skin becomes a mirror of internal fire.
When the body's Blood is chronically deficient, the skin loses its nourishment and moisture, turning dry, fragile, and poorly defended. In this state, even mild external Wind can penetrate easily and cause persistent, wandering sensitivity. This pattern is more common in people who are constitutionally weak, postpartum, or have suffered from prolonged illness.
Because each of these mechanisms - external invasion, internal heat, or blood deficiency - produces a different type of skin hypersensitivity, TCM does not treat the symptom in isolation. A practitioner looks at the quality of the redness, the presence of oozing or dryness, the tongue and pulse, and the overall constitution to determine which pattern is dominant, then tailors the herbs and acupuncture points accordingly.
classical_quote: 「银翘散主太阴风温、温热、温疫、冬温……但热不恶寒而渴者」
classical_translation: "Yin Qiao Powder governs Taiyin wind-warmth, warm heat, pestilence, winter warmth... with heat but no chills and thirst. This formula is foundational for treating Wind-Heat at the surface, which often manifests as skin hypersensitivity."
classical_source:
Wen Bing Tiao Bian (Systematized Identification of Warm Diseases)  ,  Upper Jiao 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first looks for signs of Wind-Heat when the hypersensitivity comes on suddenly with red, swollen patches and fierce itching. The skin may feel warm, and the discomfort often eases with cold compresses. The tongue is usually red with a thin yellow coating, and the pulse feels floating and rapid, confirming that an external pathogen is trapped at the surface.
When Damp-Heat is the culprit, the skin hypersensitivity tends to be accompanied by oozing, weeping, or a sticky sensation. The rash may appear as vesicles or damp erythema, and the discomfort often worsens in humid weather. The tongue body is red with a thick, greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is slippery and rapid, pointing to internal dampness combined with heat.
Heat in the Blood produces a deeper, more intense picture. The skin is bright red, feels burning hot, and may even show tiny red spots. Accompanying signs like thirst, a feeling of heat, and irritability are common. The tongue appears dark red with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse is rapid and wiry, indicating that heat has moved into the blood level and is agitating the skin from within.
For recurring or chronic hypersensitivity, a practitioner considers Blood Deficiency with External Wind. The skin is dry, scaly, and itchy, especially at night, and the person often looks pale and feels tired. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is thin and wiry or weak, reflecting an underlying lack of nourishment that leaves the skin vulnerable to wind-dryness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Red, hot, swollen skin", "Intense itching that feels worse with heat", "Sudden onset, often after a cold or sore throat", "Sore throat and thirst"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot environments, hot showers, or overheating, Greasy, spicy, fried, or sweet foods
patterns.better_with: Cool compresses or cool environment, Cool drinks or herbal teas, Rest in a cool room
patterns.why_this_happens: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen that invades the body's surface, which in Chinese medicine is governed by the Defensive Qi. When this protective barrier is disrupted, the skin becomes the battleground where heat and wind clash, causing sudden redness, swelling, and intense itching. The heat makes the skin feel hot and overly sensitive to even light touch, while the wind component makes the itching move and flare unpredictably.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip and edges with a thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen that thrives on heat and stagnation. Hot environments and spicy foods fuel the internal heat, making the skin more irritated and sensitive. Cooling measures-like cold compresses and cooling teas-counteract that heat, soothe the defensive Qi, and calm the skin's hypersensitivity.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep cool and avoid overheating. Drink plenty of water and herbal teas like mint or chrysanthemum to gently clear heat. Avoid spicy, greasy, or fried foods that add internal heat. Wear loose, breathable fabrics and use cool compresses on itchy areas.

patterns.symptoms: ["Skin feels heavy, warm, and may weep sticky fluid", "Worse in humid weather or after greasy food", "Feeling of heaviness in the body and head", "Chest and upper abdominal stuffiness", "Sticky or greasy sensation in the mouth", "Loose, sticky stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp or humid environments, Greasy, spicy, fried, or sweet foods, Alcohol or coffee, Overeating
patterns.better_with: Cool compresses or cool environment, Light, bland foods (congee, vegetables), Gentle exercise to promote sweating, Avoiding greasy and spicy foods
patterns.why_this_happens: When Dampness and Heat combine, they can become trapped in the skin, causing it to feel heavy, warm, and tender to the touch. The Dampness makes the skin swollen and may cause weeping of clear or sticky fluid, while the Heat creates redness and a burning sensation. This combination makes the skin hypersensitive to friction and pressure, and the condition often worsens in humid weather or after eating greasy foods.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow greasy coating that is thickest in the centre and root. Pulse: soggy-rapid or slippery-rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat accumulates in the body from external dampness (weather, environment) and internal dietary excess (greasy, sweet foods). These triggers add more Dampness and Heat, making the skin more swollen and sensitive. Conversely, a dry, cool environment and light, bland foods help drain Dampness and clear Heat. Gentle exercise moves Qi and opens the pores, allowing Dampness to exit through sweat, which reduces skin hypersensitivity.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, easily digestible foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and moderate amounts of cooling fruits. Avoid greasy, fried, sweet, and spicy foods that generate Dampness and Heat. Keep living spaces dry and well-ventilated; use a dehumidifier if needed. Gentle, regular exercise that produces a light sweat helps the body eliminate Dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Heat penetrates deep into the Blood, it agitates and accelerates its flow, pushing fiery energy outward to the skin. The blood vessels become engorged and inflamed, making the skin feel hot, red, and intensely sensitive to even the lightest touch. This is not a surface-level irritation but a deeper, internal heat that flares up especially when the body is at rest, as the Heat is no longer dispersed by daytime activity.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: deep red body with red spots or prickles, thin yellow dry coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shuò) and wiry (弦 xián), possibly slippery (滑 huá).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat in the Blood is a deep, internal fire that flares up when stimulated by external or internal heat sources. Spicy foods, alcohol, and emotional stress all generate additional Heat, directly worsening the skin's burning sensitivity. Conversely, cooling measures-whether through diet, environment, or rest-help drain the excess Heat and soothe the agitated Blood, calming the skin's overreaction to touch.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, alcohol, and coffee-all of which add Heat to the Blood. Instead, eat cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and chrysanthemum tea. Keep the body cool and calm; avoid hot baths, saunas, and overexertion that can stir up internal Heat. Gentle activities like walking or tai chi help move Qi without overheating.

patterns.worse_with: Wind or drafts, Dry air or low humidity, Greasy, spicy, fried, or sweet foods, Overwork or lack of sleep, Emotional stress, anger, or strain
patterns.better_with: Moisturizing the skin, Warm, calm environments, Eating nourishing, warm meals, Adequate sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's Blood is insufficient, it cannot properly nourish and moisten the skin. This leaves the skin dry, fragile, and poorly defended, making it easy for external Wind to penetrate and get trapped in the surface. The combination of internal dryness and external Wind creates a hypersensitivity where even light touch can provoke itching, and the discomfort often shifts from place to place like a gust of wind.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white and slightly dry coating. Pulse: fine (thin), often wiry at the left middle position and floating at the right front position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Deficiency leaves the skin dry and undernourished, so anything that further dries it out-like wind, dry air, or spicy foods-makes the itching worse. Wind easily invades a weakened surface, which is why drafts trigger discomfort. Nourishing foods, rest, and moisturizers replenish Blood and Yin, restoring the skin's natural barrier and making it less reactive. Calm, warm surroundings help keep the external Wind at bay and allow the body to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular meals rich in blood-nourishing foods like dark leafy greens, beets, liver, black sesame, and goji berries. Avoid cold, raw, and spicy foods that can further deplete or dry out the Blood. Protect your skin from wind and dry air with gentle, fragrance-free moisturizers and by wearing a scarf. Gentle, consistent movement like walking or tai chi helps move Qi and Blood without overexertion.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with skin hypersensitivity?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture works by calming the nervous system, reducing inflammation, and redirecting the body's Qi to expel trapped pathogens or nourish deficient Blood. Points like Quchi (LI-11) and Xuehai (SP-10) are especially effective for clearing heat and cooling the skin. Many people feel a soothing, cooling sensation during the session, and the skin often becomes less reactive over a series of treatments.

faqs.question: How quickly will I see results?
faqs.answer: That depends on the pattern. Acute hypersensitivity from Wind-Heat often starts to calm within the first few days. Damp-Heat and Heat in the Blood may take a week or two. Chronic Blood Deficiency patterns require more patience - you may notice less dryness and irritation after 2 to 4 weeks, but full rebuilding of the skin's barrier can take a couple of months.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my antihistamines or nerve pain medication?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but you must inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor. The formulas used for skin hypersensitivity are generally gentle, but some herbs like Dang Gui (Angelica sinensis) can have mild blood-thinning effects, so caution is needed if you are on anticoagulants. Never stop or adjust your prescribed medication without medical supervision.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supporting role. During a flare, it's wise to avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which can add heat and dampness. Cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and leafy greens can help. If your pattern involves Blood Deficiency, adding nourishing foods like dark leafy vegetables, red dates, and bone broths can be beneficial.

faqs.question: What if my skin is oozing or weeping?
faqs.answer: Oozing, sticky skin usually points to Damp-Heat. TCM treats this by draining dampness and clearing heat, often with herbs like Ku Shen (Sophora flavescens) and Cang Zhu (Atractylodes lancea). External herbal washes may also be used to dry and soothe the skin. It's important not to cover weeping areas with heavy creams unless advised, as this can trap dampness.

faqs.question: Will my skin sensitivity come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance, not just suppress the symptom. When the root pattern is fully resolved - whether that's clearing heat, draining dampness, or building blood - recurrences become much less likely. However, if the same lifestyle or dietary triggers that caused the imbalance continue, the sensitivity may return. A practitioner will guide you on long-term preventive habits.

research.title: Acupuncture for atopic dermatitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis of 6 RCTs found that acupuncture significantly reduced itch severity compared to placebo, but evidence for skin lesion improvement was inconclusive. The studies were small and had high risk of bias, highlighting the need for larger, well-designed trials.
research.periodical: Lee JH, Choi TY, Kim JI, et al. J Altern Complement Med. 2012;18(6): 529-536.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Xiao Feng San in treating chronic urticaria: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In a trial of 120 patients with chronic urticaria, those receiving Xiao Feng San showed a significant reduction in wheal size and itching at 4 weeks compared to loratadine, with fewer adverse events. The study supports the traditional use of this formula for wind-damp-heat skin conditions.
research.periodical: Zhang L, Wang M, Li X, et al. Chin J Dermatol. 2015;48(3): 187-190.

research.title: Dang Gui Yin Zi for chronic eczema with blood deficiency and wind-dryness: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
research.description: Eighty patients with chronic eczema were randomized to Dang Gui Yin Zi or placebo for 8 weeks. The herbal group showed greater improvement in EASI score and pruritus, with no serious adverse effects. This provides preliminary evidence for the formula's efficacy in nourishing blood and dispelling wind.
research.periodical: Wang Y, Zhao H, Liu J, et al. J Ethnopharmacol. 2018;215: 198-204.
